findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the contradiction: either fail lifespan startup (or reflect ok:False in the /health status code / a gate-readable signal) when the handshake reports ok:False, OR restate 'The defect to fix' so the goal is operator-visibility rather than blocking promotion — and add an AC proving a wrong-allowlist container is NOT promoted.
evidence: Defect: 'A container whose REBAR_MCP_HTTP_ALLOWED_HOSTS is wrong answers /health 200 while returning 421 to every real request, and the deploy promotes it and logs "mcp redeployed + healthy".'
Step 4: 'The status code stays 200 for the same reason store does.'
Step 3: '/health answering 200 then proves, by construction, that this container has already served a real MCP handshake' — but a handshake that returned ok:False is still a completed drive
AC: 'no change to infra/scripts/autodeploy.sh' — the gate still keys on 200
findings.finding: The fix does not close the 'promote-broken-container' defect the plan itself frames as the target: step 4 keeps /health at status 200 even when handshake ok:False, and AC4/step-2 say a timeout is ok:False but 'boot continues' — so a wrong-allowlist container (421, ok:False) still completes lifespan startup, answers /health 200, and is promoted, exactly the scenario 'The defect to fix' says must stop.
findings.location: 'The defect to fix' vs Fix step 3-4 and AC4
scenarios: Deploy of a container with a misconfigured host allowlist: handshake returns ok:False (421), boot continues, /health returns 200, autodeploy promotes it and logs healthy — the exact bug the plan set out to prevent
findings.suggested_fix: Add an AC that a container reporting handshake ok:False does not reach live traffic (either lifespan startup aborts, or /health signals not-ready in a way the existing gate honors), and reconcile it with the 'status stays 200' decision.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how wrap_lifespan_with_handshake reaches the inner FastMCP Starlette app's router.lifespan_context when mcp.streamable_http_app is wrapped by ProxyAuthMiddleware (mcp_server.py:663-673), e.g. wrap the lifespan before the proxy wrap or unwrap .app, so the handshake wires under the production proxy-auth config.
evidence: Plan: 'wrap_lifespan_with_handshake(app, mcp, ...) wraps the Starlette app's router.lifespan_context ... run_http_with_grace wires it.'
_mcp_health.py:314 `app = mcp.streamable_http_app()`
mcp_server.py:665-673 wraps the result in ProxyAuthMiddleware and reassigns mcp.streamable_http_app, so `app` is a middleware, not a Starlette app with `.router.lifespan_context`
findings.finding: When proxy auth is enabled, mcp_server.py:663-673 replaces mcp.streamable_http_app to return a ProxyAuthMiddleware wrapper, so the object run_http_with_grace obtains from mcp.streamable_http_app() (line 314) is a middleware instance, not a Starlette app exposing .router.lifespan_context. The plan's step 3 wraps 'the Starlette app's router.lifespan_context' and does not account for this wrapper, so the handshake wiring may not attach in the production (proxy-auth) configuration.
findings.location: Fix step 3 (wrap_lifespan_with_handshake) / run_http_with_grace in src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:314; interaction with src/rebar/mcp_server.py:663-673
scenarios: A production deploy with proxy auth enabled (auth_strategies contains 'proxy') where run_http_with_grace receives a ProxyAuthMiddleware and the lifespan-wrap targets an attribute that does not exist on it
findings.suggested_fix: Attach the lifespan wrap to the FastMCP-produced app inside the streamable_http_app factory (before ProxyAuthMiddleware wraps it), or have wrap_lifespan_with_handshake descend through the middleware's .app until it finds the object exposing router.lifespan_context.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify how wrap_lifespan_with_handshake reaches router.lifespan_context when mcp.streamable_http_app is wrapped by ProxyAuthMiddleware (mcp_server.py:663-673), given mcp_server.py is out of scope, or reach the lifespan via mcp / the FastMCP inner app rather than the returned ASGI object.
evidence: Plan: 'wrap_lifespan_with_handshake(app, mcp, ...) wraps the Starlette app's router.lifespan_context ... run_http_with_grace wires it'
src/rebar/_mcp_health.py:314 `app = mcp.streamable_http_app()`
src/rebar/mcp_server.py:663-673 replaces mcp.streamable_http_app with a wrapper returning ProxyAuthMiddleware(inner_app) when proxy auth is enabled
Plan: 'Deliberately NOT in scope: no change to ... src/rebar/mcp_server.py'
The plan's own motivation (421 on wrong REBAR_MCP_HTTP_ALLOWED_HOSTS) is an auth-enabled deploy scenario
findings.finding: The plan wraps app.router.lifespan_context on the object returned by mcp.streamable_http_app(), but when proxy auth is enabled the codebase replaces mcp.streamable_http_app to return a ProxyAuthMiddleware wrapper (not the Starlette app), which exposes no .router.lifespan_context; mcp_server.py is declared out of scope, so the handshake wrap may be unreachable in the authenticated deploy the plan targets.
scenarios: Auth-enabled HTTP deploy where mcp.streamable_http_app returns ProxyAuthMiddleware and wrap_lifespan_with_handshake tries to reach app.router.lifespan_context
findings.suggested_fix: Wrap the lifespan on the FastMCP-owned Starlette app (e.g. the inner app produced before ProxyAuthMiddleware) or key off mcp rather than the possibly-middleware-wrapped return of mcp.streamable_http_app().

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the exact StreamableHTTPSessionManager entrypoint (e.g. handle_request(scope, receive, send)) and the scope shape used, and cite the SDK signature so the synthetic-ASGI drive is a Verified surface rather than Partially-verified.
evidence: Plan: 'drives ONE real initialize JSON-RPC request through the server's own StreamableHTTPSessionManager with a synthetic ASGI scope'
StreamableHTTPSessionManager resolves (EXISTS), but its request-drive method (e.g. handle_request) was UNRESOLVED via symbol probe (not proof of absence)
Existing tests drive requests only via Starlette TestClient over app = server.streamable_http_app() (test_mcp_http_transport.py:113-127), never by calling the session manager directly
Plan design note #2 ('the ASGI receive yields the body once and then http.disconnect ... verified') implies the author probed it but the entrypoint is unnamed
findings.finding: The plan asserts it drives ONE initialize JSON-RPC request through the server's own StreamableHTTPSessionManager with a synthetic ASGI scope, but does not name the concrete session-manager entrypoint used; the existing codebase drives MCP requests only via Starlette TestClient over the full ASGI app, so this direct session-manager drive is a new/unverified SDK surface.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the chosen `budget_seconds` value and confirm total startup (import + handshake budget) stays within the container HEALTHCHECK start-period and the blue-green gate's wait window, so the added handshake cannot itself cause a deploy timeout.
evidence: 'the handshake runs AFTER session_manager.run() is entered and BEFORE uvicorn reports application startup complete'
'5.5-7.5 s of Python process startup before uvicorn binds'
Absence: no stated relationship between budget_seconds and the container HEALTHCHECK start-period / autodeploy readiness wait
findings.finding: The handshake runs synchronously inside the ASGI lifespan BEFORE uvicorn reports startup complete and thus before the process is HEALTHCHECK/ready, adding up to `budget_seconds` on top of the already-measured 5.5-7.5 s Python startup. The plan does not state how `budget_seconds` relates to the container's docker HEALTHCHECK start-period/interval or the blue-green gate's wait window, so a large budget on a slow-importing container could push total startup past the HEALTHCHECK deadline and cause the deploy to time out instead of promoting.
findings.location: Fix step 3 (wrap_lifespan_with_handshake) and Acceptance Criteria: 'a drive that exceeds budget_seconds is reported as ok: False, and boot continues'
scenarios: A container that imports slowly plus a generous budget_seconds exceeds the HEALTHCHECK start-period; the orchestrator marks the container unhealthy and the redeploy fails or rolls back even though the server would eventually serve.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Reconcile the title with the RCA: reframe the headline around the readiness-contract defect (premature promotion of a not-yet-serving container) and add an end-state acceptance criterion that the first client connecting immediately after promotion succeeds, since latency itself is explicitly not being reduced.
evidence: Title: 'First MCP initialize after a redeploy exceeds 30s, so the first client to connect always fails'
'A cold authenticated initialize ... completes in 0.030 s. The reported 8.43 s does not reproduce'
'No attempt to shorten the 5.5 s import cost -- that is a separate, larger piece of work and this change makes it harmless rather than faster.'
findings.finding: The title attributes the first-client failure to `initialize` exceeding 30 s, but the investigation refutes that (cold initialize = 0.030 s) and the fix explicitly does NOT reduce the 5.5 s startup latency ('No attempt to shorten the 5.5 s import cost'). The delivered change fixes the readiness CONTRACT (premature promotion of a not-yet-serving container), not initialize latency. The end-state proof that 'the first client no longer fails' is implied by the lifespan ordering but is not stated as an explicit acceptance outcome, leaving the headline promise ('first client always fails') only indirectly tied to the fix.
scenarios: A reader takes the title literally and expects a latency reduction; the plan instead changes the readiness signal, so the headline and the delivered work describe different mechanisms.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Declare the access posture of the new /health `handshake` field (public-unauthenticated, matching `store`) and confirm the `handshake.error` text is a bounded, non-sensitive summary rather than raw internal detail.
evidence: _mcp_health.py:213-217 register_health_route docstring: 'route lives on the Starlette app OUTSIDE the auth and transport-security middleware — an unauthenticated probe gets 200'
Fix step 1: handshake returns '{"ok", "status", "elapsed_ms", "budget_ms", "error"}'
store_status already returns `path` and `error` text unauthenticated (_mcp_health.py:163), so this is a continuation of an established posture, not a new boundary — hence advisory
findings.finding: The new /health `handshake` field adds an `error` string (and status/timing) to an endpoint the plan itself confirms is unauthenticated (register_health_route: 'an unauthenticated probe gets 200'); the plan does not state what the handshake `error` string may contain, so an internal exception/message could surface to any unauthenticated probe. This mirrors the pre-existing store.error exposure, so it is advisory rather than a new boundary — but the plan should DECLARE the access posture of the new field and confirm the error text carries no sensitive internal detail.
findings.location: Fix step 4 (`/health` gains a `handshake` field) and AC '`/health` reports the handshake result alongside in_flight and store'
scenarios: An unauthenticated caller of /health reads handshake.error and learns internal configuration/exception detail (e.g. the allowlisted Host value or a stack-ish error string)
findings.suggested_fix: State in the Fix section that `handshake.error` is a short bounded status summary (no allowlist secrets/raw tracebacks), consistent with the existing unauthenticated /health posture.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Justify the synthetic-ASGI-scope drive through StreamableHTTPSessionManager against the MCP SDK's in-memory client (Client(mcp)) and the established readiness-via-handshake pattern, explicitly stating that the in-memory client is rejected because it would bypass the HTTP transport-security/host-allowlist guard that AC line 3 requires the probe to exercise.
evidence: Plan: 'run_startup_handshake(mcp, *, budget_seconds) drives ONE real initialize JSON-RPC request through the server's own StreamableHTTPSessionManager with a synthetic ASGI scope'

Retrieved MCP blog (blog.modelcontextprotocol.io, 2026-07-28): 'pass your MCPServer instance directly to Client (async with Client(mcp) as client:) and it connects in memory, the same pattern as FastAPI's TestClient' — a supported SDK in-process handshake driver the plan does not mention

Retrieved prior art (Health Monitor MCP Server, mcpservers.org): 'Instead of pinging a port, it calls list_tools on each server — the same handshake your agent uses — so a green status means the server is actually ready' — establishes the readiness-via-handshake pattern the plan reinvents
resolve_symbol confirms mcp.client.session.ClientSession is importable in this environment, so the SDK alternative is real and available

The plan's own AC line 3 (transport-security host allowlist must refuse the probe with 421) supplies the likely justification for rejecting an in-memory client, but the plan never states this trade-off
findings.finding: The plan chooses a bespoke readiness mechanism (a synthetic ASGI scope driven manually through StreamableHTTPSessionManager with hand-managed receive/http.disconnect) without considering the two pieces of directly relevant prior art: (a) the MCP Python SDK's supported in-memory client (Client(mcp), documented as 'the same pattern as FastAPI's TestClient') which drives a real initialize handshake in-process, and (b) the established readiness-via-handshake pattern used by existing MCP health tooling (calling the real handshake instead of pinging a port). The plan has a strong reason to prefer its own approach — the in-memory client would bypass the HTTP transport-security/host-allowlist guard that AC line 3 makes central — but that rejection rationale is never stated, so the novel mechanism is unjustified against the alternative.
findings.location: Fix step 1-2 (run_startup_handshake: 'drives ONE real initialize JSON-RPC request through the server's own StreamableHTTPSessionManager with a synthetic ASGI scope')
scenarios: Reviewer/maintainer cannot tell whether the synthetic-ASGI-scope approach was chosen deliberately over the SDK in-memory client or simply overlooked
A future maintainer replaces the hand-rolled drive with the in-memory client and silently loses the transport-security/421 coverage that is the plan's stated point
findings.suggested_fix: Add a short 'why not the SDK in-memory client' note to Fix step 1: the in-memory Client(mcp) transport connects at the session layer and does NOT traverse the Starlette HTTP app, so it cannot exercise the DNS-rebinding transport-security host/origin guard — which is precisely the 421 path AC line 3 requires the probe to prove; the synthetic ASGI scope is chosen for that reason.
